titleStmt.title: COLOURED PETRI NET MODELLING OF REAL-TIME TASK SCHEDULING

analytic.title: COLOURED PETRI NET MODELLING OF REAL-TIME TASK SCHEDULING

div.p: Embedded computers are widely used to perform functions with real-time constraints. Such real-time computer systems typically use separate tasks for implementing independent functions, requiring a run-time system to schedule tasks for execution. Confirming that tasks satisfy their real-time constraints is possible using schedulability analysis for single processor systems where system design has been suitably constrained. However, where system design uses complex inter-task interactions, or asynchronous task arrival times, or multiple processors, it becomes difficult to verify that tasks will satisfy real-time constraints.

A generic Coloured Petri Net model has been developed to support analysis of the run-time behaviour of real-time systems. The model accommodates multiprocessor architectures with tasks statically bound to processors, and without restrictions on inter-task communications. First application of the model has been to the mission computers of a Seahawk helicopter, to test model applicability to a complex multiprocessor system. The model was successfully used to verify real-time constraints on task executions for system operation in a single scenario. Inherently high complexities associated with scheduling problems remain a challenge to successful modelling, and there is a risk of modelling being computationally infeasible for some systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Embedded computers are deployed in many domains, commonly in uniprocessor configurations, and often with real-time constraints to satisfy. Military applications for embedded computers include mission systems, where large-scale functionality is required and real-time constraints apply. Mission system applications can require multiple processors with large software loads to meet functionality and timing requirements.
For mission systems, and other applications where correct system operation is critical, system operation must be fully verified before deployment.

Mission systems are also subject to long service lifetimes required from military assets, during which changes to operational environments can precipitate modifications to mission system functionality. Multiple change cycles may apply during the life of the system, and each will require re-verification of system operation.

Verifying the correct real-time operation of embedded multiprocessor computers can be a significant challenge. Through schedulability analysis of system design, it may be possible to confirm that system operation will satisfy real-time constraints, if system design has adhered to constraints required by the analysis. This is not always possible or desirable, and alternative means of verification are required. Run-time tests and measurements can confirm timing properties of a system, but it may not be feasible to fully cover all operational possibilities required for a complete verification. Modelling system real-time behaviour provides another means to analyse system operation, and can provide confirmation that real-time constraints are satisfied by the system design.

System designs that have been constrained to have all tasks arrive synchronously, and that observe restrictions such as a strictly rate monotonic task prioritisation, can be analysed for schedulability using the results of Liu and Layland [1], and of Lehoczky et. al. [2]. Relaxation of restrictions on prioritisation order and deadline times has occurred in response time analysis methods reported by Audsley et al. [3] and Tindell [4]. Multiprocessor systems, and systems that permit asynchronous task arrivals, remain difficult to analyse due to their inherent complexity, as discussed by Leung and Whitehead [5]. Modelling of system hardware and software architectures has been investigated as a means to support analysis of systems not readily analysed by other means. Coloured Petri Nets (CPNs) provide a modelling capability for timed concurrent discrete event systems that was found to be suitable for the implementation of a model.

div.head: 6C1-2
div.p: A generic CPN model was developed as a tool for modelling real-time task scheduling on embedded multiprocessor systems. The model is generic in that it does not model a specific system architecture, instead accepting a parameterised description of a system to configure the model. This generic model has been used to model the mission system of the S-70B-2 Seahawk helicopter, and model results have been confirmed against measurements taken from operational Seahawk mission computers. This paper introduces CPN modelling, presents an overview of the generic CPN model, discusses the application of the model to the Seahawk mission system, and demonstrates analysis supported by the model.

div.head: Coloured Petri Nets
div.p: CPNs use a graphical notation for model construction, and have an underlying algebraic representation for efficient CPN execution [6,7]. Modularisation is supported to assist with construction of large CPN models, and complex data types and data manipulations can be used. Computer tools assist with model construction, execution and analyses. The Design/CPN tool, produced by the CPN group at the University of Aarhus in Denmark, was used to construct the CPN model described in this paper, and to execute the model with the tool's inbuilt simulator.

CPN models describe the states that a system may be in, and the conditions under which state changes happen. Concurrency is supported by CPNs, so that multiple state variables can change at the same modelled instant of time. The graphical notation for CPNs uses a directed graph with two types of nodes, referred to as places and transitions. Directed arcs are used to form connections between nodes, and data values called tokens can reside on place nodes.

Place nodes are used to store model state, and are assigned a colour which is a data type for tokens that can reside on the place. Place nodes may be assigned initial tokens that will reside on the place at model start-up, or can default to having no initial tokens. Place nodes can be designated to be members of a fusion group, which allows a single place node to appear on multiple pages for implementing functionality that spans model pages. It is also possible to designate place nodes to be ports, which are used to form a connection between a model page and a sub-page in a modularised CPN model.

Transition nodes determine the manner in which token values can be altered to change model state. When a transition changes the state of the model, the transition is said to occur. A transition can only occur when it is enabled, which requires that tokens be available on all input arcs to the transition. Transitions may also have a guard expression, which must evaluate to a Boolean true for the transition to be enabled. When a transition occurs it removes tokens on its input arcs, and generates tokens on its output arcs. Specialised transitions known as substitution transitions are used to implement modularisation, by forming interfaces to sub-pages drawn as separate model pages. Transitions may optionally have a code segment associated with them, which can contain Standard Meta Language (SML) instructions to be executed each time the transition occurs.

Arcs are used to form connections between nodes, and can only connect places to transitions or transitions to places. Input arcs connect places to transitions, and output arcs connect transitions to places. Annotations are attached to arcs to describe token values, or to indicate bindings of tokens to model variables.

Tokens are assigned to belong to a colour set, which is their data type. Tokens can only reside on places of the same colour, with any number of tokens being able to reside on a single place. Enablement times may be given to tokens, to block their availability for enabling transitions until a certain model time is reached.

Design/CPN uses a tailored subset of the SML functional programming language for performing data manipulations within CPN models. Where complex data structures or manipulations are required, SML functions can be defined outside of a CPN diagram to preserve diagram clarity. A simulated model time is also provided by the Design/CPN environment for modelling time dependent functionality. Figure 1 shows a sample of the CPN graphical notation with an identification key.

div.head: Generic Real-Time System Model
div.p: The generic CPN model was developed to be able to model a range of mission computer hardware and software architectures. Application to a specific system architecture involves development of a parameterised description of system hardware architecture, software task set and run-time scheduling protocol.

The model was constructed using substitution transitions to partition the model into a number of separate pages. Parameters describing the system being modelled are not stored within the model, but are instead read from a file during system initialisation.

As the model is executed, CPN transition occurrences and bindings of token values to model variables are logged in a report file. Information of direct interest for task scheduling is also written to the report file by commands placed in transition code segments, for use in post execution analysis.
Discussion of the entire model is not possible due to its size, so key model pages are presented in the following paragraphs to reflect choices made for model design.

div.head: Generic AMS Model Page
div.p: The top level structure for the model is contained in the Generic_AMS model page, shown in Figure 2. Parameterised data is read and processed during model initialisation, and used to create tokens on fusion group place Task_Descriptions. A sub-page of substitution transition Task_Initialisation removes tokens from the Task_Descriptions place, and generates tokens for all modelled tasks on either the Periodic_Task_Control_Data or Aperiodic_Task_Control_Data places.

div.head: Task Sequencing Page
div.p: The Task_Sequencing model page is shown in Figure 3. Tokens on place Ready_Tasks are assigned to processor, I/O or sleep resources to model a task operation. Tasks perform sequences of operations, and may be assigned to different resources many times during a single execution.

The sleep resource is used to model tasks not wanting processor or I/O resources for a specific period of time. The Sleep transition is enabled for such tasks with tokens on place Ready_Tasks. Occurrence of the Sleep transition puts a token onto place In_Progress_Tasks with an enablement time corresponding to the end of the sleep period.

div.head: Figure 3. Task_Sequencing Model Page
div.p: Ready tasks requiring a processor resource will satisfy the guard condition on the Compute transition, enabling it to occur and put a token onto the Compute_Tasking place. The Task_Compute substitution transition sub-page will then be enabled to model processor resource usage. At the conclusion of processor usage modelling, a token is put onto place In_Progress_Tasks.

Ready tasks requiring an I/O resource will satisfy the guard condition on the Input_Output transition, enabling it to occur and put a token onto the IO_Tasking place. The Task_Input_Output sub-page models task I/O operations, after which a token for the task will be put back onto place In_Progress_Tasks.
At the conclusion of a processor, I/O or sleep resourced operation, the token on place In_Progress_Tasks will satisfy the guard condition on either the Complete or the Incomplete transition.

div.head: 6C1-5
div.p: A task with more operations to be modelled will enable the Incomplete transition, and a token will be put onto the Ready_Tasks place. Otherwise, the Complete transition will be enabled and a token will be put onto place Executed_Tasks.

div.head: Task Enqueueing Page
div.p: The Task_Enqueueing page implements modelling of processor ready queues, and is shown in Figure 4. A token is put onto fusion group place Ready_Queue during model initialisation for each processor being modelled.

div.head: Figure 4. Task_Enqueueing Model Page
div.p: A token on place Ready_Tasks will enable transition Enqueue to occur if task processing is not currently in progress and the required ready queue token is available on place Ready_Queue. Otherwise, transition Interrupt will be enabled if the executing task is preemptable or may not have started execution. After occurrence of transition Interrupt a token is put onto place Interrupted, and one of the transitions Reschedule or Resume, which have complementary guard conditions, will be enabled. Transition Reschedule will occur if the interrupted task was preemptable or had not started, adding the task from place Ready_Tasks to the ready queue it puts onto place Ready_Queue. Transition Resume will occur if the interrupted task was not preemptable and had started, and the task on place Ready_Tasks will not be able to join the ready queue until execution of the non preemptable task completes.

When a ready queue token on place Ready_Queue contains at least one task, the Start transition is enabled and can put a ready queue token onto place Processing_Queue. A token on place Processing_Queue enables modelling of task operations within the Task_Processing sub-page and its nested sub-pages. On completion of modelling task operations, a ready queue token is returned to the Ready_Queue place, and a task token is output to the Processed_Tasks place if the task has completed processor resourced operations.

div.head: Model Application to the Seahawk
div.p: Initial applications of the generic CPN model were to uniprocessor and small scale multiprocessor systems that were useful for testing model operation, but were not representative of real-world systems. Application of the model to a large scale real-world mission system was desired to demonstrate the abilities and scalability of the modelling approach. The mission system of the S-70B-2 Seahawk was selected as the candidate for modelling due to its multiprocessor architecture and substantial mission processing functionality.

Two mission computers are used in the Seahawk to provide redundancy, each of which contains three processors to meet mission computing workload demands. A dual redundant MIL-STD-1553 databus connects the mission computers to each other and to other mission 6C1-6 avionics. The three processors in a mission computer all run multiple tasks, and engage in inter-task communications through the use of shared memory and inter-processor interrupts. Task scheduling is performed by run-time executives on each processor that schedule application tasks to run on the basis of fixed task priorities, with temporary priority changes being allowed for deadlock avoidance.

Importing the Seahawk mission system architecture into the generic CPN model required the collection of parametric information describing system hardware, software and I/O architectures. Hardware architecture was determined in terms of the six processors being used in the mission computers. Software architecture was determined in terms of the software tasks being executed, task bindings to processors, task processing time requirements, task priorities, execution frequencies for periodic tasks, inter-task communications and the task scheduling protocol used by the system executive. System I/O architecture was determined in terms of MIL-STD-1553 databus messages and the message schedule. Much of this information was available in system documentation, but some had to be determined by referring to system software source code. Measurements were conducted on operational Seahawk mission computers to determine task execution times.

The length of mission system operation that it was necessary to model was determined by the period that elapsed before the system schedule repeated previously visited states. A section of the infinite system schedule sufficient to contain all possible schedule behaviour has been defined as a partial schedule by Leung and Whitehead [3]. The length of a partial schedule is twice the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of all task periods, and grows exponentially where task periods do not have common factors. For a system of the complexity of the Seahawk, model execution times of hours or days can be expected due to the large numbers of task state calculations involved, following from the sensitivity of partial schedule length to the LCM of task periods. Model execution was performed for the partial schedule of the Seahawk using the built in simulator of the Design/CPN tool.

After model execution, it remained to be verified that the model was operating correctly. An initial test that could identify the presence of inconsistencies between modelled behaviour and measured Seahawk behaviour was the total utilisation of each mission computer processor. Modelled and measured total processor utilisations were found to differ by less than 0.02%, giving initial confidence in model operation. Modelled and measured processor utilisations for each task were then compared to verify that individual tasks were correctly utilising processor resources. Small discrepancies of the order of 0.02% were traceable to the effects of rounding errors on task execution time measurements for tasks that were executed large numbers of times during the partial schedule. This close level of agreement between modelled and measured behaviours gave confidence that the model was correctly modelling Seahawk mission computer operation.

During CPN model execution, state information was recorded in a report file for subsequent extraction and use in post-processing steps. Post-processing of the report file was used to determine worst-case response times for tasks. Worst-case task response times that exceed task deadlines indicate schedule failures, which would lead to task overruns or task shedding. Response times for periodic tasks were directly measured by the CPN model and recorded in the log file. Post-processing of the log file was used to derive worst-case response times for aperiodic tasks, which use inter-task communications to control their executions rather than the periodic arrival times and completion times that the generic model uses to calculate response times.

Although dependencies on inter-task communications have introduced execution delays in addition to the preemption delays associated with fixed priority scheduling, no periodic or aperiodic tasks were found to have worst-case response times that exceeded their deadlines. This result confirms, for the mission scenario in which task execution times were measured, that no task scheduling failures occur at any time in the infinite task schedule of the Seahawk mission computers. If a worst-case response time had been found to exceed a deadline, the model could have been used to examine the circumstances leading to the condition so that contributing factors could be fully understood.

div.head: 6C1-7
div.p: Model output can also be used to generate timing diagrams to assist with comprehension of task schedules. Timing diagrams show when tasks are active and consuming processor resources, and can identify preempting tasks responsible for delaying the execution of a lower priority task. Figure 5 shows an example timing diagram of Seahawk mission computer task scheduling over a period of two seconds. Seahawk mission computer task executions were modelled to a one microsecond resolution, so that task scheduling behaviour could be examined in closer detail using a scale as small as microseconds where necessary.

div.head: Figure 5. Modelled Task Schedule
div.p: Several uses are evident for the generic CPN model. Being able to confirm that a real-time system will correctly schedule tasks for execution is of critical importance when verifying that a system is fit for service. In a system that experiences schedule failures, the model could be used to develop understanding of the causes of the failures, and to test potential solutions. The model is also useful in being able to test the schedulability of changes proposed for a system before making investments in their implementation, allowing early decisions on change feasibility. Additional analysis is being developed to use the model to determine system sensitivity [8], so that margins can be identified within which task timings can be changed without affecting run-time schedulability.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: A generic CPN model has been developed and successfully applied to modelling the mission system of the Seahawk helicopter. This has involved modelling six processors, more than sixty software tasks, and over six thousand MIL-STD-1553 messages per databus frame. Model operation has been verified to be in agreement with measurements taken from operational Seahawk mission computers.

The model has been used to perform a response time analysis for Seahawk mission system tasks, confirming for a specific scenario that all periodic and aperiodic tasks complete their operations before their deadlines. A sensitivity analysis is being developed to determine margins by which task execution times can be altered while still guaranteeing system schedulability.

A fundamental limitation of the model is its sensitivity to the LCM of task periods, which could potentially result in unreasonable model execution times. However, for many real world mission systems the LCM of task periods will not be excessive, and was not an issue for modelling the Seahawk mission system.
